items.deviations: I added the four extra refusals above because the differential check showed the record's rules accepting frontmatter that strict parsers read differently or refuse. PyYAML, which skill-creator's quick_validate.py uses, refuses tabs after a colon or at the end of a line. The parser's own regexes now match spaces only, not [ \\t]. The key message now reads 'frontmatter key must start with a letter and not read as a YAML boolean, null or number: <line>'.

review_findings.problem: The whitelist parser stores keys on a plain object (`const data = {}`). A top-level `__proto__` key therefore hits the prototype setter and is never an own key. A scalar `__proto__: x` is dropped silently, which also skips the not-portable-key and duplicate-key checks. A bare `__proto__:` with nested lines becomes the prototype, so a nested `name` is inherited and passes the name checks. The result is that validate.mjs, and the whole root chain, accepts a SKILL.md that every strict YAML parser reads with no top-level `name` and an unknown `__proto__` key, which claude.ai and the Skills API reject. This contradicts the new header comment ('A small YAML subset that strict YAML parsers and Claude Code read the same way') and 76a's 'unique keys' rule. The nested level is safe, because KEY refuses `__proto__` there.
review_findings.outcome_evidence: parseFrontmatter's maps are created with Object.create(null), so __proto__ is an own key: the 'not portable' error and the name checks fire. New row with '__proto__:\n  name: prompt-engine' expects both. It fails with a plain {} restored.

findings.title: install.md tells users to build the skill zip with release.mjs --zip, which needs a zip binary that stock Windows lacks
findings.summary: docs/install.md:63 tells users to run `node scripts/release.mjs --zip` and names no prerequisites. release.mjs:36-37 runs the external `zip` and `unzip` commands. Without them it passes validate, then crashes with an unhandled `spawnSync zip ENOENT` stack trace, exit 1 and an empty dist/; I reproduced this with PATH=/nonexistent. Stock Windows has no `zip` (Microsoft documents tar.exe and Compress-Archive). Git for Windows adds `unzip` and GNU tar but not `zip`. Both facts come from docs; no Windows machine was available. The repo has 0 releases and 0 tags, so today the zip must be built.

findings.title: The npm README says the npm package doesn't exist yet, and each published version will keep saying it
findings.summary: mcp/README.md:16 says the npm package and the .mcpb "appear with the first release" and tells readers to build from a clone. That file goes into the npm tarball unchanged. npm only refreshes a package page's README when a new version is published, and neither version.mjs nor the release steps touch the line. So D20's 0.0.1 placeholder, and then 0.1.0 (published in the same workflow run as the GitHub release), would both show it until the next version. The registry part is overstated: the official registry stores only metadata and links to the live mcp/ folder on GitHub, so a fix on main reaches those readers without a new version.

claims.claim: mcp/README.md:16 says the npm package and the .mcpb appear with the first release, and to build from a clone until then.
claims.evidence: mcp/README.md:16: "The npm package and the `.mcpb` file appear with the first release. Until then, build from a clone ...". It is the first paragraph under "## Install" (:14).

claims.evidence: I extracted $S/pkg/prompt-engine-mcp-0.1.0.tgz: package/README.md:16 has the line, and `cmp` against HEAD's mcp/README.md shows they're identical. prepack only runs license.mjs (mcp/package.json:49), so nothing rewrites the README.

claims.claim: npmjs.com changes a package page's README only when a new version is published.
claims.evidence: docs.npmjs.com/about-package-readme-files, fetched 2026-11-06: "The README.md file will only be updated on the package page when you publish a new version of your package."

claims.claim: D20's 0.0.1 placeholder carries the line: the rehearsal at .claude/CLAUDE.md:46 runs version.mjs, which leaves it alone.
claims.evidence: In a git-archive copy, `node scripts/version.mjs 0.0.1` changed only plugin.json, mcp/manifest.json, package-lock.json, package.json, server.json, content.ts and SKILL.md; mcp/README.md:16 was unchanged. version.mjs:41-73 edits only version fields. Today `npm view prompt-engine-mcp` still returns E404, so 0.0.1 hasn't been published yet.

claims.claim: 0.1.0 is published in the same run that creates the GitHub release.
claims.evidence: release.yml:36 `gh release create`, then :53 `npm publish`, in one job. At HEAD the npm step skips when there's no NPM_TOKEN (:49-52), and the repo has no secrets. D15 moves CI to trusted publishing. Under D16's four-job split the two steps become separate jobs of the same run.

claims.claim: From 0.1.0 on, both halves of the sentence are false, and the page keeps the line until the next npm version.
claims.evidence: Follows from the three claims above. Nothing in docs/publishing.md:26-64 removes the line: `grep -n -i "first release\|README" docs/publishing.md` finds only :87, the HTTP hosting link.

claims.claim: The MCP Registry entry points to the same file (server.json:11, subfolder mcp).
claims.evidence: server.json:8-12 gives the repo URL with subfolder "mcp" and no ref, and the schema calls it the URL "for browsing source code". The registry's add-package-registry.md:3 says it "hosts metadata for MCP servers but does not host the code". Its npm validator (internal/validators/registries/npm.go) reads mcpName and never the README. So registry readers land on the live copy on main, not on a frozen copy. What third-party front-ends display wasn't checked.

claims.claim: npm-page and registry readers are told to build from a clone instead of using the npx line just below.
claims.evidence: It holds for the npm page. Registry readers see it only while main still has the line, which makes them the same audience as GitHub readers.

findings.refutation:
I tried to refute the finding six ways:
1. Does anything rewrite the README when packing or publishing? No. Only LICENSE is copied in.
2. Is this already covered by finding 37? 37 lists :16 among its locations, but its claims cover the caveat before publication, and its fix leaves the line in place. So this extends 37 with new evidence: the line is frozen into each npm version.
3. Could a by-hand 0.1.0 publish before the tag (publishing.md:20) make the line briefly true? Only the .mcpb half, and only until the tag's workflow creates the release.
4. Does the registry freeze the README? No (see the registry claim).
5. Severity. Nothing is frozen yet: the npm name returns E404, there are no releases, and main is the initial commit. The npx lines follow right below, so readers can still get it working. Minor stands.
6. The checked_ok note. The homepage (mcp/package.json:16, tree/main/mcp) does return 404 today, but it fixes itself at merge because it points at main. mcp/README.md has no relative file links (only anchors and two absolute links, both 200), so the "relative README links 404" part doesn't apply to this file.

audit.reasoning: The defect is real. mcp/README.md:16 says the npm package and the .mcpb "appear with the first release" and tells readers to build from a clone. That file goes into the npm tarball unchanged. npm only refreshes a package page's README when a new version is published. Neither version.mjs nor any release step removes the line. No step 1a fix removes it either: 37's fix #4 applies only if the owner merges before claiming the name, and D20 claims it now. So the 0.1.0 page, published in the same workflow run as the GitHub release, would carry a false line until 0.1.1. The registry part is overstated, as the verifier said. Registry entries hold only server.json metadata, and server.json points at the live mcp/ folder, so a fix on main reaches registry readers without a new version. Severity minor, close to trivial, because the npx lines follow right after. Not an owner decision: the fix is just new wording. It extends 37 and doesn't repeat it.

findings.title: Nothing installs and runs the packed npm package before it ships, so a broken package passes every gate
findings.summary: Nothing installs and runs the packed npm package. release.mjs has no --dry-run and boots only the esbuild-bundled MCPB. Every runtime test runs dist/cli.js inside the source tree. When I moved @modelcontextprotocol/node to devDependencies, 233 tests, the Inspector gates and the MCPB check all passed, yet both the installed package and npx failed with ERR_MODULE_NOT_FOUND. Three secondary claims are overstated: a missing LICENSE leaves a package that runs (the license text is missing, nothing breaks), the published dist bytes are the ones the tests ran, and `npm publish` does warn when the bin file is missing.

claims.claim: plan.md:135 plans a release.mjs --dry-run that runs npm pack and boots the packed entry on Node 22 and 24.
claims.evidence: The text is there; it dates from 34d9caa, and D26 changed the Node versions. plan.md:91 also lists "release (--dry-run|--publish)". "The packed entry" could mean the MCPB's entry, which is how 1a's finding 32 read it.

claims.claim: release.mjs has no --dry-run; it reads only --zip and --tag.
claims.evidence: The only options are release.mjs:24 value('--tag') and :43 flag('--zip'). Unknown flags are ignored, so `--dry-run` would run the full build.

claims.claim: release.mjs never packs or starts the npm package; it boots only the MCPB, through pack:mcpb.
claims.evidence: release.mjs:48-56 runs only `npm run pack:mcpb`. pack-mcpb.mjs:72-83 starts the bundle, which esbuild built from src (bundle.mjs:15-29).

claims.claim: The only check on the npm package is manifests.test.ts:43-53, which lists the files with --ignore-scripts.

findings.refutation:
I tried to refute the finding six ways:
1. Could any existing gate catch a misplaced dependency? I checked tsc, vitest, the Inspector gates, the MCPB check (esbuild bundles devDependencies too), the Worker smoke test and validate.mjs. None does.
2. Does npm warn on its own? npm pack is silent for all three breaks. npm publish warns only about the missing bin.
3. Could a documented path ship the no-build tarball? No. Every one builds first.
4. Does D16 make things worse? No. Today's prepublishOnly also tests the source tree, not the tarball.
5. Is this already covered by findings 19 or 32? No: 19 is about unit tests for the scripts, and 32 about release gating.
6. Severity. The current package installs and runs on npm 11.19 with Node 24, over both stdio and --http, so this is a missing safety net. But npm versions can't be reused, and a broken latest version reaches every npx user until a new one is published. Minor stands.

audit.reasoning:
Reproduced in my own clone. With @modelcontextprotocol/node moved to devDependencies:
- All 233 tests pass, all 32 Inspector gates pass, and the MCPB check passes.
- npm pack gives 11 files and no warning.
- The installed package fails with ERR_MODULE_NOT_FOUND, both through npm install and through npx.
No gate installs the tarball. Every runtime test uses dist/cli.js in the source tree. The MCPB is an esbuild bundle, so it hides dependency sections. manifests.test.ts:46 packs with --ignore-scripts, and ci.yml:57 and CLAUDE.md:27 only print a list. plan.md:135 (approved, written in 34d9caa) asks for npm pack and a boot of the packed entry, and release.mjs has neither. So no owner decision is needed.
The verifier's three corrections hold:
- A missing LICENSE doesn't break npx; the server runs.
- The tested dist bytes are the published ones (shasum identical before and after release.mjs).
- npm publish does warn when the bin file is missing.
No current documented path ships the no-build tarball. Severity minor: the gap is latent, and today's package works over stdio and --http on Node 24. Not a repeat: 19 covers unit tests for the scripts, and 32 covers release gating.

findings.title: release.mjs says the MCP Registry lists the .mcpb with its SHA-256, but server.json lists only the npm package
findings.summary: The comment at release.mjs:58 says SHA256SUMS exists because the MCP Registry lists an .mcpb with its SHA-256. But server.json lists only the npm package, the registry step never reads SHA256SUMS, and an .mcpb listing would take its hash from server.json's fileSha256, not from this file. No doc tells users how to check a download. It's a comment, so the severity is trivial.

claims.claim: The comment gives the MCP Registry as the reason for SHA256SUMS.
claims.evidence: release.mjs:58: "// 4. Checksums (the MCP Registry lists an .mcpb package with its SHA-256)." It has been there since 7fb1b1a.

claims.claim: server.json has a single package, of registryType npm.
claims.evidence: server.json:13-23 has one package. `git log -S mcpb -- mcp/server.json` finds nothing, so it never listed one.

claims.claim: manifests.test.ts:72-74 requires exactly that list.
claims.evidence: It asserts toEqual with a one-element array: registryType 'npm', identifier pkg.name.

claims.claim: The registry step never reads SHA256SUMS.
claims.evidence: release.yml:54-69 has the wait loop, the mcp-publisher download, login and publish, and nothing else. SHA256SUMS appears only at :38, as a release asset.

claims.claim: No doc tells users how to verify downloads.
claims.evidence: `git grep -n -i SHA256SUMS` finds release.mjs:60, release.yml:38, docs/publishing.md:11 (an asset list) and the review JSON.

claims.claim: A maintainer would think registry clients can find and verify the bundle.
claims.evidence: The comment's statement is true of the registry in general. The schema says fileSha256 is "Required for MCPB packages", and package-types.mdx:255 says the same. But as the reason for this file it doesn't apply: there's no mcpb listing, and plan.md:40 sends the .mcpb out "via GitHub Releases". The effect is limited to maintainers reading the code.

findings.refutation:
I tried four ways:
1. Reading the comment as a general fact about the registry. It is accurate as such, but it still doesn't explain this file.
2. History. server.json never listed an mcpb package, and nothing in plan.md plans a registry listing.
3. Severity. It's a comment, with no runtime or user effect, so I lowered it from minor to trivial.
4. Context. GitHub already shows a SHA-256 for each release asset, so users have another way to check.
No step 1a finding covers it.

audit.reasoning: The comment at release.mjs:58 gives the MCP Registry as the reason for SHA256SUMS. But server.json lists only the npm package, and has never listed an mcpb one. manifests.test.ts:72-74 pins that, and the registry step never reads the file. Even an .mcpb listing would carry its hash in server.json's fileSha256, not in SHA256SUMS. No user doc explains how to check a download. It's only a comment, so trivial, as the verifier set it.
